chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abbas ibn Amir, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about one who leaves his home with falcons, hawks, and dogs to go for a leisure trip for one night, two nights, or three nights: does he shorten his prayer or not? He said, 'He has gone out for leisure, so he does not shorten.' I said, 'A man escorts his brother for one day or two days in the month of Ramadan?' He said, 'He breaks his fast and shortens [his prayer], for that is a right upon him.'
ai.seo_question: Does a short trip for leisure count as travel for shortening prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the distinction between travel for necessity and travel for leisure is clarified: a trip for hunting or sport is considered 'lahw' (frivolous) and does not qualify for prayer shortening, whereas a brief escort journey in Ramadan permits both breaking fast and shortening prayer. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that the intent and nature of the journey, not just distance, determine the ruling of safar. The hadith underscores the flexibility in applying travel concessions even for short durations when the purpose is legitimate social duty.
